text: What is Git?

options.text: A cloud hosting service for websites

text: Which of these best describes a Git repository?

options.text: A database that only Git's servers can access
A directory tracked by Git that stores the full history of a project
A single file containing all project code
A backup folder created automatically by the operating system

text: What is the main difference between Git and a centralized version control system like SVN?

options.text: Git only works with text files, SVN works with any file
Git requires an internet connection for every operation
In Git every clone has a full copy of the project history, not just the latest snapshot
SVN supports branching, Git does not

text: What is GitHub in relation to Git?

options.text: GitHub is another name for the same program as Git
GitHub is a hosting platform for Git repositories with added collaboration features
GitHub is required to use Git locally
GitHub is a command inside Git

text: Which command shows the installed Git version?
What does the 'working directory' (working tree) in Git refer to?

options.text: The folder where Git itself is installed
The remote server that stores the repository
The current set of files on disk that you are editing

text: What is the '.git' folder?

options.text: A temporary cache that can be safely deleted at any time
The hidden directory where Git stores all repository metadata and history
A folder that contains only ignored files
The folder shown on GitHub's website

text: Which area in Git sits between the working directory and the repository history, holding changes prepared for the next commit?
What uniquely identifies a Git commit?

options.text: The file name that was changed
A SHA-1 (or SHA-256) hash of its contents and metadata

text: Which command displays the current state of the working directory and staging area?
Which command sets your Git username globally for all repositories?
What does 'git init' do?

options.text: Downloads a repository from a remote server
Initializes a new, empty Git repository in the current directory

text: Which file lets you tell Git which files or folders to never track?
Where is a repository-specific (local) Git configuration typically stored?
What is the purpose of 'git config --global core.editor'?

options.text: To choose which text editor Git opens for commit messages and interactive operations
To set the default branch name
To pick the default merge tool only
To configure the remote repository URL

text: Which command stages a specific file for the next commit?
Which command stages all changed and new files in the current directory?
What does 'git commit -m "message"' do?

options.text: Stages all files and pushes them to the remote
Records the staged changes as a new commit with the given message
Merges the current branch into main

text: What does the '-a' flag do when used with 'git commit -a -m "..."'?

options.text: Automatically stages all tracked, modified files before committing
Aborts the commit if there are conflicts
Adds a tag to the commit

text: Which command shows the commit history of the current branch?
Which command shows the differences between the working directory and the staging area?
How can you see the differences between the staging area and the last commit?
What does 'git commit --amend' do?

options.text: Deletes the last commit permanently with no trace
Creates a brand-new branch from the last commit
Modifies the most recent commit, e.g. to fix its message or add staged changes
Pushes the last commit to the remote again

text: Why is it recommended to avoid amending a commit that has already been pushed and shared with others?

options.text: Amending is always technically impossible after a push
It rewrites history, which can cause conflicts for collaborators who already have the original commit
It permanently deletes the remote repository

text: Which command removes a file from the working directory and stages the deletion?
What is a Git branch?

options.text: A copy of the repository stored on a different server
A movable pointer to a specific commit, representing an independent line of development

text: Which command creates a new branch called 'feature'?
Which command creates a new branch called 'feature' AND switches to it in one step?
What is 'HEAD' in Git?

options.text: The name of the main branch
A pointer that usually references the tip of the currently checked-out branch
The very first commit of the repository
A file that lists all remote branches

text: What does a 'detached HEAD' state mean?

options.text: HEAD points directly to a specific commit instead of to a branch
The repository has no commits yet
The remote repository has been deleted
The current branch has been merged and removed

text: Which command lists all local branches?
Which command lists both local and remote-tracking branches?
Which command deletes a local branch named 'feature' that has already been merged?
What is the difference between 'git branch -d' and 'git branch -D'?

options.text: There is no difference, they are aliases
-D forces deletion even if the branch has unmerged changes; -d refuses to delete in that case
-d deletes local branches, -D deletes remote branches
-D only works on the main branch

text: Which modern command is recommended for switching between existing branches (introduced as a clearer alternative to 'git checkout')?
What does 'git merge feature' do when run on the main branch?

options.text: Integrates the changes from the feature branch into the current branch
Uploads the feature branch to the remote

text: What is a 'fast-forward' merge?

options.text: A merge that combines three or more branches at once
A merge where the current branch pointer is simply moved forward because there is no divergent history
A merge that is performed automatically by GitHub Actions
A merge that skips running any hooks

text: When does Git create a merge commit instead of doing a fast-forward merge?

options.text: Whenever git merge is used, always
When the branches have diverged (both have commits the other doesn't)
Only when merging with a remote repository

text: What causes a merge conflict?

options.text: Two branches change the same lines of a file (or one edits, one deletes) in different ways
Two branches have completely unrelated files
The repository has more than one remote
A commit message is too long

text: In a file with merge conflict markers, what does the section between '<<<<<<< HEAD' and '=======' represent?

options.text: The changes from the branch being merged in
The changes from the current branch (HEAD)
Lines that will be deleted automatically

text: After manually resolving a merge conflict in a file, what should you do next?

options.text: Delete the .git folder and start over
Stage the resolved file with 'git add' and then complete the merge with 'git commit'
Nothing, Git detects the resolution automatically without staging

text: Which command aborts an in-progress merge and returns to the state before the merge started?
What does 'git rebase main' do when run on a feature branch?

options.text: Replays the feature branch's commits on top of the latest main branch, creating a linear history
Merges main into feature using a merge commit

text: What is a key difference between merging and rebasing?

options.text: Merge creates a merge commit and preserves branch history; rebase rewrites commits to create a linear history
Rebase can only be used with remote branches
Merge is only for bug fixes, rebase is only for features

text: Why is rebasing commits that have already been pushed and shared considered risky?

options.text: It permanently deletes the remote repository
It rewrites commit history, which can cause conflicts and confusion for others who already pulled the original commits
It is not risky at all
Git does not allow pushing after a rebase under any circumstance

text: What does an interactive rebase ('git rebase -i') allow you to do?

options.text: Reorder, squash, edit, or drop commits before they are replayed
Automatically resolve all merge conflicts without review
Convert the repository from Git to SVN

text: What does 'squashing' commits during an interactive rebase mean?

options.text: Deleting commits without any trace in the reflog
Combining multiple commits into a single commit
Splitting one commit into several smaller commits
Pushing commits to multiple remotes at once

text: Which command continues an interactive rebase after resolving a conflict?
What does 'git clone <url>' do?

options.text: Creates an empty repository with the given name
Downloads a full copy of a remote repository, including its history, to your local machine
Copies only the current branch's latest file snapshot with no history
Uploads your local repository to a new remote

text: What is the conventional name Git gives to the remote a repository was cloned from?
Which command lists the remotes configured for a repository along with their URLs?
What is the difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?

options.text: They are identical in every way
'git fetch' downloads new commits from the remote without merging them; 'git pull' fetches and then merges (or rebases) into the current branch
'git pull' only works on the main branch
'git fetch' also pushes local commits to the remote

text: Which command uploads local commits on the current branch to the remote repository?
What does 'git push -u origin feature' do?

options.text: Deletes the feature branch from the remote
Pushes the feature branch to origin and sets up tracking so future 'git push'/'git pull' know the default remote branch
Pushes the feature branch but forces overwrite of remote history

text: What is the purpose of adding an 'upstream' remote when working with a forked repository?

options.text: To point to your own fork so you can push your changes
To reference the original repository you forked from, so you can pull in its latest changes

text: Which command adds a new remote named 'upstream' pointing to a given URL?
What typically happens if you try to 'git push' and the remote branch has commits that you don't have locally?

options.text: Git silently overwrites the remote branch
Git rejects the push and asks you to fetch/pull and integrate the remote changes first

text: What does 'git push --force' do, and why is it considered dangerous on shared branches?

options.text: It pushes tags only; it is completely safe
It overwrites the remote branch's history to match your local branch, potentially discarding others' commits
It merges the remote branch into local automatically
It only affects your local repository, never the remote

text: What does 'git checkout -- <file>' (or 'git restore <file>') do?

options.text: Discards uncommitted changes in the working directory, restoring the file to its last committed state
Creates a new branch from the file

text: What does 'git reset --soft HEAD~1' do?

options.text: Deletes the last commit and all its changes permanently
Undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged
Undoes the last commit and unstages the changes, keeping them in the working directory
Removes the last commit from the remote repository

text: What does 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' do?

options.text: Undoes the last commit but keeps the changes in the working directory
Undoes the last commit and discards its changes completely from the working directory and staging area
Only unstages files without touching commits
Creates a backup branch automatically before resetting

text: What is the key difference between 'git reset' and 'git revert' for undoing a commit?

options.text: They do exactly the same thing
'git reset' moves the branch pointer and can rewrite history; 'git revert' creates a new commit that undoes the changes, preserving history
'git reset' only works on remote branches

text: Why is 'git revert' generally safer than 'git reset' for undoing changes on a shared/public branch?

options.text: It does not rewrite existing history, so it won't conflict with what collaborators already have
It permanently deletes the unwanted commit

text: Which command removes untracked files from the working directory?
If you accidentally staged a file you didn't mean to, which command unstages it while keeping your edits?
What does 'git restore --staged <file>' do?

options.text: Deletes the file from the working directory
Unstages the file, moving its changes back to the working directory only
Restores the file from the last tag

text: What is the purpose of 'git stash'?

options.text: To temporarily save uncommitted changes so you can work on something else, then reapply them later
To create a new remote repository
To squash all commits into one

text: Which command reapplies the most recently stashed changes and removes them from the stash list?
What is the difference between 'git stash apply' and 'git stash pop'?

options.text: 'apply' reapplies the stash and keeps it in the stash list; 'pop' reapplies it and removes it from the list
'pop' only works on the main branch
'apply' deletes the stash without reapplying it

text: Which command lists all currently stashed changesets?
What is a Git tag typically used for?

options.text: Marking a specific commit as important, such as a release version (e.g. v1.0.0)

text: Which command creates an annotated tag named 'v1.0' with a message?
What is the difference between a lightweight tag and an annotated tag?

options.text: A lightweight tag is just a pointer to a commit; an annotated tag is a full object with a message, author, and date
Lightweight tags can only be created on the main branch
Annotated tags cannot be pushed to a remote

text: Which command pushes all local tags to the remote repository?
If a file matches a pattern in '.gitignore' but was already tracked by Git before the pattern was added, what happens?

options.text: Git continues to track it; .gitignore only affects previously untracked files
The file is deleted from disk
.gitignore is ignored entirely if any tracked files match

text: Which command shows a compact, one-line-per-commit history with a branch graph?
What does 'git show <commit-hash>' display?

options.text: The metadata and the actual changes (diff) introduced by that specific commit
A list of all branches containing that commit

text: What is 'git blame <file>' used for?

options.text: Deleting a file and blaming the last author
Showing which commit and author last modified each line of a file
Reverting a file to its original state

text: What does 'git cherry-pick <commit-hash>' do?

options.text: Deletes the specified commit from history
Applies the changes introduced by a specific commit from another branch onto the current branch
Creates a tag pointing to that commit

text: What is the purpose of 'git bisect'?

options.text: To split a branch into two new branches
To perform a binary search through commit history to find which commit introduced a bug

text: What is the 'reflog' in Git?

options.text: A log of all files ever ignored by .gitignore
A local record of where HEAD and branch references have pointed over time, useful for recovering lost commits
The commit history shown on GitHub's website
A list of all remote repositories

text: A commit was accidentally lost after a 'git reset --hard'. Which tool can often help recover it?
What does 'git log --author="name"' do?

options.text: Changes the author of all commits to 'name'
Filters the commit history to show only commits by the given author
Creates a new branch owned by that author

text: In a typical feature-branch workflow, what is a 'pull request' (or 'merge request')?

options.text: A Git command that pulls changes from a remote
A request, usually made on a hosting platform like GitHub, to merge changes from one branch into another, often with review and discussion
A way to delete a remote branch

text: What does 'forking' a repository on a platform like GitHub mean?

options.text: Creating your own personal copy of someone else's repository on the platform, so you can make changes independently
Splitting one repository into two unrelated ones locally

text: What is a Git 'submodule'?

options.text: A smaller branch inside the main branch
A reference to another Git repository embedded at a specific path and commit within a parent repository
A private, encrypted section of a repository

text: What are Git 'hooks'?

options.text: Scripts that Git runs automatically before or after events like commit, push, or merge
Special branches used only for releases
A way to hide files from 'git status'

text: Which command shows only the file names that differ between two commits, without the full diff content?
What does 'git log -p' show in addition to the commit list?

options.text: The full patch (diff) introduced by each commit
A performance report of the repository

text: Why is it good practice to write a clear, descriptive commit message?

options.text: Git requires a minimum message length or it rejects the commit
It helps collaborators (and your future self) understand the history and reason behind each change
Commit messages are compiled into the application
It automatically fixes any bugs introduced
